newsitem.title: INDIA: Daylight reveals full horror of India mid-air crash.
newsitem.headline: Daylight reveals full horror of India mid-air crash.

text.p: Daylight revealed the full horror of the world's worst mid-air disaster on Wednesday as experts debated how a Saudi jumbo and Kazakh cargo plane collided near New Delhi, killing 351 people.

Rescuers worked overnight, using tractor-trolleys to cart away most of the 312 charred and mangled bodies, including women and children, from the wreckage of the Saudi Arabian Airlines Boeing 747 lying in mustard and chickpea fields 80 km (50 miles) southwest of the Indian capital.

The wreckage of the plane, which a policeman said hit the ground in three pieces, was still smouldering early on Wednesday. The main section of the fuselage, its roof ripped off, was barely recognisable.
Only the tail section of the Saudi aircraft, carrying mostly Indian and Nepali workers and pilgrims to the Moslem holy land, was reasonably intact.
Seats stood upright, dinner trolleys and unbroken crockery sat forlorn in the fields as rescue workers tramped past suitcases, letters and photographs scattered in the dirt.
Some suitcases were empty and local people said there had been looting.
"It's very sad that people here behave in this manner," local businessman Vinod Garg told Reuters as police tried to keep people off the sprawling crash site.
Local governments declared a day of mourning. Schoolgirls said they assembled for a two-minute prayer for the victims and then were sent home.
The Indian army spent the night building a helipad and setting up communications, and soldiers were expected to be drafted in to help on Wednesday, officials said.

The wreckage of the Kazakh Airlines Ilyushin Il-76 that had been preparing to land at Delhi's Indira Gandhi International airport, carrying 28 passengers and 10 crew, lay some 10 km (six miles) away after colliding with the jumbo.
The Saudi plane had just taken off for Dharan and Jeddah.
An American military pilot reported seeing a bright light in the sky he initially thought was lightning, then two fireballs descending to earth.
Policeman Kanwar Singh, who said he was the first person to reach the point where the jumbo plunged into the ground leaving a 20-foot (six-metre) crater, also saw a fireball in the sky.
"I saw the fireball and I started following the plane. I heard a big bang," he said.

Housewife Krishna Devi said she was cooking dinner at her outdoor kitchen in the village of Kheri Sanwal as darkness descended on Tuesday evening and that she believed the pilot of the Saudi plane appeared to be trying to avoid the houses.
"I saw the plane circle this area twice. It was on fire," she told Reuters.
Police said they had been told to concentrate on rescue work and not search for the flight and cockpit recorders that should explain what went wrong.
Civil aviation experts would sift the wreckages for those and other vital clues, they said.
A variety of possible explanations were on offer, ranging from inadequate equipment at Delhi airport to pilot misunderstanding of ground controller instructions.
Top Indian civil aviation officials said the Saudi plane was cleared to climb to 14,000 feet after taking off and the Kazakh freighter had been told to stay at 15,000 feet, a normal separation.
But someone, somewhere made a mistake that led to the mid-air collision.
One possibility, experts said, was that Delhi's ageing radar was not up to pinpointing exact positions and altitudes of converging aircraft, although its busy airport has a good safety record.

One unnamed expert quoted by the Asian Age newspaper said the pilot of the Kazakh plane may have misunderstood instructions given in English, the language of international aviation. He said saying pilots from the former Soviet Union often had difficulty understanding the language.
